title: LLM2Rec: Large Language Models Are Powerful Embedding Models for Sequential Recommendation

problem.claim: Sequential recommendation must model collaborative filtering signals from historical user or item behaviors to predict future interactions.

gap.claim: ID-based embeddings lack transferable knowledge for unseen domains, while text-based approaches fail to encode collaborative filtering signals.

contributions.claim: LLM2Rec is an embedding model for sequential recommendation that integrates LLM semantic understanding with collaborative filtering awareness.
LLM2Rec uses collaborative supervised fine-tuning followed by item-level embedding modeling to produce item embeddings encoding semantic and collaborative information.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly characterize LLM2Rec as a novel embedding model tailored for sequential recommendation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments on real-world datasets improve recommendation quality in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.
The authors report that their findings indicate potential for LLMs to build more robust and generalizable embedding models for sequential recommendation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Sequential recommendation relies on collaborative filtering signals from historical behaviors.
ID-based embeddings do not transfer well to unseen domains, while text-based representations omit collaborative filtering signals.
An ideal embedding model should combine collaborative filtering signals with rich semantic representations.
LLM2Rec combines LLM semantics and collaborative awareness through two-stage training.
The authors report improved recommendation quality across in-domain and out-of-domain settings.

source_observation.claim: Combining semantic representations with collaborative signals may address the complementary weaknesses of ID-based and text-based recommendation models.

interpretation.claim: Recommendation representations can benefit from integrating transferable semantic knowledge with behavior-derived relational information.

application.claim: For sequential recommendation, consider training representations that jointly encode item semantics and historical interaction structure.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which datasets, domains, baselines, or conditions determine when this integration is beneficial.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative effect sizes.
The abstract does not describe computational cost, limitations, or failure cases.
